questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a niche market?
options: A small, specialised segment of a larger market with distinct needs
A market served by only one very small business
A market in a single country only
A market for very expensive products
questions.why: The defining feature is specialisation, not size of the firm or the price charged.
whyNot: The business serving a niche may be large.
A niche can be global.
Price is not the defining feature.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a global niche market?
options: A niche too small to be viable in one country that becomes viable when served in many
A market for products sold in every country in the world
The largest segment of a global market
A market served only through exports
questions.why: Going global is therefore the way an unviable niche becomes a viable business, which is the core of this topic.
whyNot: That would be a mass market.
A niche is by definition not the largest segment.
The route to market is not the definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines cultural diversity?
options: The existence of different interests, values and behaviours among groups across the world
The number of languages spoken in a country
The proportion of a workforce born abroad
The variety of products available in a market
questions.why: Because groups hold different interests and values, there are specialised needs that no mass-market product serves.
whyNot: Language count is one narrow indicator.
That is workforce composition.
That is product choice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a niche market?
options: Lower price sensitivity, so premium pricing is usually possible
Very high price sensitivity, forcing low prices
Large volumes in each country
Intense competition from mass-market firms
questions.why: Customers who cannot get the product elsewhere will pay for it, so margins are high.
whyNot: Niche customers are typically less price sensitive.
Volumes in each country are small.
Large firms usually judge the segment too small to bother with.

questions.stem: What made global niche markets reachable at acceptable cost?
options: Search, social media and e-commerce, which allow direct international selling
The reduction of tariffs by the WTO
The growth of trading blocs
The standardisation of shipping containers
questions.why: Reaching 0.5% of forty countries used to require distributors and marketing in forty countries, which cost more than the niche was worth.
whyNot: Tariff reductions helped trade generally but did not solve the reach problem.
Blocs help regional trade rather than dispersed niche customers.
Containers cut bulk shipping cost, not the cost of finding niche customers.

questions.stem: What is the main barrier to entry protecting a niche business?
options: Specialist expertise rather than scale
Very large production capacity
Government licensing in every market
Ownership of national distribution networks
questions.why: The knowledge required to serve the niche well is what protects it.
whyNot: Scale is the mass-market barrier.
Licensing applies to particular regulated sectors.
Niche businesses usually sell direct rather than through national networks.

questions.stem: Which is the defining practical problem of a global niche?
options: Customers are geographically dispersed, so logistics and returns are costly
Customers are unwilling to pay a premium
Competitors are numerous and aggressive
The product must be adapted for every country
questions.why: Shipping cost and time to many countries, customs paperwork and international returns can consume the margin on small orders.
whyNot: Niche customers are usually willing to pay a premium.
Direct competition is typically limited.
The specialism itself is what the customer wants, so heavy adaptation is unusual.

questions.stem: Which promotional channel is most valuable for a global niche?
options: Word of mouth within the interest community
National television advertising
Billboards in major cities
Mass-market print advertising
questions.why: It cuts both ways, because a niche community also circulates complaints quickly.
whyNot: Broad media reach mostly people outside the niche.
Outdoor advertising is untargeted.
Mass-market print is similarly untargeted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a niche strategy?
options: Limited total size, so growth eventually stops
Very low margins on every sale
High promotional cost per customer reached
The impossibility of premium pricing
questions.why: The niche is finite, which is a real constraint on a business that needs to keep growing.
whyNot: Niche margins are usually high.
Targeted promotion is cheap per relevant customer reached.
Premium pricing is normally available.

questions.stem: Why is focus both the strength and the risk of a niche strategy?
options: Everything depends on one segment continuing to exist
Focus prevents the business from making a profit
Focus always means very high costs
Focus removes the need for any marketing
questions.why: A change of fashion or technology removes the whole market, and there is nothing to fall back on.
whyNot: Focus is usually highly profitable in a niche.
Costs depend on the product, not on focus itself.
Targeted marketing is still required.

questions.stem: Why is a growing niche not a safe niche?
options: If it grows enough, a mass-market firm may enter with far greater resources
Growth always raises the cost of production
Niche customers become more price sensitive as a market grows
Growth removes the need for specialist expertise
questions.why: Success attracts entrants, which is why the protection of a niche is never permanent.
whyNot: Growth usually improves scale, not worsens it.
Sensitivity depends on the competition that arrives, not on growth itself.
Expertise remains the basis of the offer.

questions.stem: Why do niche businesses not benefit from economies of scale?
options: Volumes stay small, so unit costs stay high and the strategy depends on the premium price holding
Niche products are always handmade
Scale economies are only available to exporters
Niche businesses refuse to grow
questions.why: This is why a niche strategy is a poor fit for a business whose advantage is scale.
whyNot: Many niche products are manufactured conventionally.
Scale economies depend on volume, not on export status.
They grow within the limits of the niche.

questions.stem: Which business is a global niche strategy least suited to?
options: One whose competitive advantage is scale and low cost
One with genuine specialist expertise
One able to sell and ship internationally online
One with a distinctive, highly specialised product
questions.why: The strategy suits expertise-based advantage, not cost-based advantage.
whyNot: That is exactly the profile it suits.
That capability is a requirement for the strategy.
That is exactly the profile it suits.

questions.stem: Why is delivered price a particular concern for a global niche business?
options: Shipping, duty and returns can be a large proportion of a small order
Niche customers will not pay any delivery charge
Duty is charged at a higher rate on niche products
International orders cannot be priced in advance
questions.why: Free returns on international orders can eliminate the margin entirely.
whyNot: Many will pay, but the cost still erodes the margin.
Duty depends on the goods, not their niche status.
Prices can be set in advance.

questions.stem: Why can a specialist diving operator in a small island economy be a good example of a global niche?
options: The segment is tiny in any one country and substantial worldwide, and marketing runs through specialist communities
Diving holidays are a mass-market product
The operator competes on price with general tour operators
Demand is unaffected by economic conditions
questions.why: High margins and high concentration of risk sit together, since demand depends on long-haul discretionary spending and on the reef itself.
whyNot: It is a specialised segment, not a mass market.
It competes on specialisation, not price.
Long-haul discretionary demand is highly cyclical.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines premium pricing?
options: Setting a price above the market average to reflect quality, exclusivity or specialisation
Setting a price below cost to gain market share
Charging different prices in different countries
Setting a price equal to the market leader's
questions.why: It is normally available in a niche because competition is limited and demand is relatively inelastic.
whyNot: That is destroyer or predatory pricing.
That is price discrimination.
That is competitive or going-rate pricing.
